Let \(p\) be any prime, \(K\) any field of characteristic \(p\), and
\(\lambda\) an integer with \(0\leq\lambda<p\).
Let \(V(\lambda)\) be the complex irreducible highest-weight
\(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)\)-module of highest weight \(\lambda\),
of dimension \(\lambda+1\). Its Chevalley generators satisfy

\[
[h,x]=2x,\qquad[h,y]=-2y,\qquad[x,y]=h.
\]

Choose a nonzero highest-weight vector \(v\) with \(xv=0\) and
\(hv=\lambda v\). Let \(U_{\mathbb Z}\) be the integer subalgebra of
the universal enveloping algebra generated by all divided powers
\(X_r=x^r/r!\), \(Y_r=y^r/r!\), for integers \(r\geq0\).
An **admissible lattice** \(M\subset V(\lambda)\) is a free abelian
subgroup with an integer basis that is also a complex basis, stable under
\(U_{\mathbb Z}\). It is arbitrary, not necessarily the minimal lattice.

Put \(V(K)=M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\). The Lie algebra
\(L(K)=(\mathbb Zx+\mathbb Zy+\mathbb Zh)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\)
acts by the induced lattice operators. This is the Chevalley
\(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) construction also in characteristic 2.
Prove that \(V(K)\) is nonzero and every \(K\)-linear subspace
invariant under \(x,y,h\) is zero or all of \(V(K)\).
Both \(\lambda=0\) and \(p=2\) are included; \(K\) need not be
algebraically closed.
value.conclusion: V_K is nonzero, and for every K-linear subspace W of V_K invariant under the induced x,y,h operators, W={0} or W=V_K. Thus V_K is irreducible as a module for the stipulated Chevalley Lie algebra L_K.

parameters.type: Z-submodule of the underlying additive group of V

hypotheses.statement: 0≤lambda<p, with lambda and p compared in Z.
V is the complex irreducible highest-weight sl2(C)-module of highest weight lambda, with the given action x,y,h, and dim_C V=lambda+1.
hx−xh=2x, hy−yh=−2y, and xy−yx=h as complex-linear endomorphisms of V; products mean composition, rightmost first.
M is an arbitrary admissible lattice in V: it has a Z-basis whose images under inclusion form a complex basis of V, and it is stable under U_Z. No minimal-lattice condition is imposed.

definitions.definition: ell=max(lambda,0), viewed as a natural number (Int.toNat lambda).
n=ell+1. Index sets below are I_n={0,...,ell}, equivalently Fin n. In scalar expressions ell−2i is integer subtraction.
For every natural r, X(r)=X_r=(r!:C)^(-1) x^r. Here 0!=1 and the zeroth operator power is Id_V.
For every natural r, Y(r)=Y_r=(r!:C)^(-1) y^r.

definitions.type: integer subalgebra of U(sl2(C)) acting on V
definitions.definition: U_Z is exactly the integer subalgebra of the universal enveloping algebra generated by every divided power x^r/r! and y^r/r! for natural r; its represented generators on V are X_r,Y_r.
V_K=V(K)=M⊗_Z K, with K-scalar action on the second tensor factor. Tensor products are algebraic, generated additively by pure tensors subject to additivity and Z-balancing.
U=K⊗_Z M, with K-scalar action on the first tensor factor.

definitions.type: predicate on a subspace and an endomorphism over a field
definitions.definition: For any field k0, k0-vector space U0, subspace W0 and k0-linear endomorphism f0, Stable(W0,f0) means for every w0∈W0 one has f0(w0)∈W0. Invariance is this predicate.
For i∈Fin(n), e_i=(i!:C)^(-1)y^i v. This formula defines vectors without yet claiming independence.
X_M(r)=X_r^M is the restriction of X_r to M; admissibility supplies its preservation of M.
Y_M(r)=Y_r^M is the restriction of Y_r to M.
x_M=X_M(1), the restriction of x.
y_M=Y_M(1), the restriction of y.
h_M=x_M y_M−y_M x_M. Its identification with the restriction of h is proved internally.
c_j=choose(ell,j), the natural binomial coefficient.
Q_M=Y_M(ell) X_M(ell).
A_ij=X_M(ell−i) Q_M Y_M(ell−j), for indices i,j∈Fin(n); the displayed subtractions are natural and nonnegative.
Dprod=∏_{j∈Fin(n)} c_j.
d_j=∏_{k∈Fin(n), k≠j} c_k; an empty product is 1.

For f∈End_Z(M), define the K-linear operator F(f) by F(f)(a⊗m)=a⊗f(m). The rule is additive and Z-balanced in a,m, so the tensor universal property defines an additive operator, and multiplication on the first factor makes it K-linear. This defines a function, with its ring-homomorphism laws to be proved separately.
S(m⊗a)=a⊗m, extended additively by the tensor universal property: the displayed rule is additive in each input and Z-balanced. K-linearity and bijectivity are proved internally.
S_inv(a⊗m)=m⊗a, defined by the same additive Z-balanced universal property.
red(t) is the image of the integer t in K; for natural t use its integer image first. A bar over an integer or natural denotes red. It preserves finite sums, products and 1.
T_ij=red(c_j)^(-1)·F(A_ij). Field inverse is the usual total inverse (0^(-1)=0); nonvanishing needed for cancellation is proved internally.
ind(f) is the induced lattice operator on V_K, given by ind(f)(m⊗a)=f(m)⊗a. The additive Z-balanced rule defines the operator and is K-linear by the scalar action on the second factor.

L_Z is the free abelian group on the three abstract Chevalley generators, denoted x,y,h in the original problem, with Z-bilinear alternating bracket [h,x]=2x, [h,y]=−2y, [x,y]=h. In formulas for the action, the parameter endomorphisms x,y,h are the respective images of these generators; the integral Lie algebra is not defined as their possibly nonfaithful image in End_C(V).

L_K=L(K)=L_Z⊗_Z K=(Zx+Zy+Zh)⊗_Z K in the original Chevalley notation, with the bracket extended K-bilinearly from the integral bracket. The action on V_K assigns the formal generators the operators ind(x_M),ind(y_M),ind(h_M) and extends K-linearly. Its bracket-preserving property is proved separately. This definition includes characteristic 2.

import Mathlib

namespace YuiBasisObjects

noncomputable def dividedPower {V : Type*} [AddCommGroup V] [Module ℂ V]
    (f : Module.End ℂ V) (r : ℕ) : Module.End ℂ V :=
  ((r.factorial : ℂ)⁻¹) • f ^ r

def Stable {K V : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V]
    (W : Submodule K V) (f : Module.End K V) : Prop :=
  ∀ w, w ∈ W → f w ∈ W

structure AdmissibleLattice (n : ℕ) (V : Type*) [AddCommGroup V] [Module ℂ V]
    (x y : Module.End ℂ V) where
  carrier : Submodule ℤ V
  zBasis : Module.Basis (Fin n) ℤ carrier
  cBasis : Module.Basis (Fin n) ℂ V
  coe_basis : ∀ i, (zBasis i : V) = cBasis i
  stableX : ∀ (r : ℕ) (m : V), m ∈ carrier → dividedPower x r m ∈ carrier
  stableY : ∀ (r : ℕ) (m : V), m ∈ carrier → dividedPower y r m ∈ carrier

end YuiBasisObjects

universe uK uV

namespace Reduction
open scoped BigOperators
open YuiBasisObjects
variable {V : Type*} [AddCommGroup V] [Module ℂ V]
noncomputable def e (y : Module.End ℂ V) (v : V) (i : ℕ) : V :=
  (i.factorial : ℂ)⁻¹ • (y ^ i) v
def c (ell : ℕ) (j : Fin (ell + 1)) : ℕ := Nat.choose ell j.val
def Dprod (ell : ℕ) : ℕ := ∏ j : Fin (ell + 1), c ell j
def d (ell : ℕ) (j : Fin (ell + 1)) : ℕ :=
  ∏ k : Fin (ell + 1), if k = j then 1 else c ell k
def hM {M : Type*} [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℤ M]
    (XM YM : ℕ → Module.End ℤ M) : Module.End ℤ M :=
  XM 1 * YM 1 - YM 1 * XM 1
def A {M : Type*} [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℤ M]
    (XM YM : ℕ → Module.End ℤ M) (ell : ℕ)
    (i j : Fin (ell + 1)) : Module.End ℤ M :=
  XM (ell - i.val) * (YM ell * XM ell) * YM (ell - j.val)
noncomputable def AC (x y : Module.End ℂ V) (ell : ℕ)
    (i j : Fin (ell + 1)) : Module.End ℂ V :=
  dividedPower x (ell - i.val) *
    (dividedPower y ell * dividedPower x ell) * dividedPower y (ell - j.val)
def VK (K M : Type*) [Field K] [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℤ M] :=
  TensorProduct ℤ M K
def pure (K : Type*) {M : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℤ M]
    (m : M) (a : K) : VK K M := TensorProduct.tmul ℤ m a
noncomputable instance vkAdd (K M : Type*) [Field K] [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℤ M] :
    AddCommGroup (VK K M) := inferInstanceAs (AddCommGroup (TensorProduct ℤ M K))
noncomputable def swapAdd (K M : Type*) [Field K] [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℤ M] :
    VK K M ≃+ TensorProduct ℤ K M :=
  letI : Module ℤ (TensorProduct ℤ M K) := TensorProduct.instModule
  letI : Module ℤ (TensorProduct ℤ K M) := TensorProduct.instModule
  (TensorProduct.comm ℤ M K).toAddEquiv
noncomputable instance vkModule (K M : Type*) [Field K] [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℤ M] :
    Module K (VK K M) := (swapAdd K M).module K
noncomputable def swap (K M : Type*) [Field K] [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℤ M] :
    VK K M ≃ₗ[K] TensorProduct ℤ K M :=
  (swapAdd K M).linearEquiv K
noncomputable def F (K : Type*) {M : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℤ M]
    (f : Module.End ℤ M) : Module.End K (TensorProduct ℤ K M) := f.baseChange K
noncomputable def ind (K : Type*) {M : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℤ M]
    (f : Module.End ℤ M) : Module.End K (VK K M) :=
  (swap K M).symm.toLinearMap ∘ₗ F K f ∘ₗ (swap K M).toLinearMap
noncomputable def T (K : Type*) {M : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup M] [Module ℤ M]
    (XM YM : ℕ → Module.End ℤ M) (ell : ℕ)
    (i j : Fin (ell + 1)) : Module.End K (TensorProduct ℤ K M) :=
  (c ell j : K)⁻¹ • F K (A XM YM ell i j)
def MatrixUnits {k : Type*} [Field k] {U : Type*} [AddCommGroup U] [Module k U]
    (n : ℕ) (t : Fin n → Fin n → Module.End k U) : Prop :=
  (∀ i j a b, t i j * t a b = if j = a then t i b else 0) ∧
  (∑ j, t j j) = 1
end Reduction

F is the native LinearMap.baseChange function; the pinned Module.End.baseChangeHom RingHom projection supplies its already checked algebraic implementation without a fresh dependency theorem. The terminal statement concerns all K-linear subspaces of the original tensor order. T012 checks the Chevalley identities and equivalence to invariance under all linear combinations of formal generators, including characteristic 2. 32: open the exceptional independent B-final review below. A faithful result then has
33: `AUDIT-B-CONDITIONAL`, a freeze-deviation warning and an explicit harness-defect
34: report. Invalid native evidence, incomplete dependencies or changed provenance
35: cannot be overridden semantically. Nonfaithful/unverified results wait for the
36: three explicit user choices in [proof repair](proof-repair.md); accepting a different
37: result does not complete the original target. Explicit/manual legacy semantic
38: receipts remain supported under their original schemas and are not relabeled.
39: Explicitly nonindependent/self-review records remain readable development checks;
40: they cannot grant whole-workflow Audit B acceptance. The same qualification rule
41: applies to supplied Audit A authority and incremental producer/cut reviews.
42: 
43: ## Author correspondence explanations
44: 
45: During interface authoring, provide `endpoint_correspondence`, keyed by every
46: E ID and P. Each entry is `{mode: direct|equivalent, explanation: string}`.
47: Keep it short and useful; do not restate the entire proof or manufacture a
48: line-by-line formalization commentary:
49: 
50: - **Direct:** identify the corresponding variables, hypotheses and assertion.
51:   One sentence is enough when the translation is immediate.
52: - **Equivalent:** explain the mathematical identification or reformulation,
53:   why it works in both directions and which existing conditions it uses.
54:   Point to relevant definitions or checked conversions when needed.
55: 
56: For example, expressing invariance under a finite basis of operators can encode
57: invariance under their linear span: explain the spanning property and closure
58: of a subspace under linear combinations. The review must establish those facts
59: for the actual source algebra/action; the word “equivalent” alone is insufficient.
60: 
61: The postprocessing author carries these notes into each E/P entry in
62: `mapping.json`, checks them against the actual export and completes missing
63: notes for older frozen contracts. It must not change frozen proof statements
64: or bodies merely to improve a note. An explanation is an author's claim, not
65: an Audit B verdict or a formal proof.
66: 
67: ## Semantic responsibility before freeze or at explicit B-final
68: 
69: Read the explanation together with the original source statement and actual
70: elaborated Lean type. Follow the definitions needed to interpret the endpoint,
71: including structure fields that might hide extra assumptions. Check each E/P
72: row, then these four global checks:
73: 
74: 1. `endpoint_inventory_and_scope`: all original E statements and P are covered;
75:    the source version, reviewer scope and inherited qualifications are explicit.
76: 2. `external_statement_fidelity`: each external assumption has the source's
77:    complete mathematical meaning, including conditions and quantifiers. With
78:    no external inputs, record that fact.
79: 3. `complete_target_and_representations`: the entire target theorem has the
80:    same meaning, including every hypothesis. Validate the explanation of each
81:    direct or equivalent encoding and relevant edge cases.
82: 4. `kernel_closure_and_trust`: the actual exported proof compiled, all required
83:    producers and intermediate library ports were discharged, and the checked
84:    root has only the declared external assumptions and permitted foundations.
85: 
86: Equivalent formulations are allowed. Do not reject a faithful encoding because
87: it lacks a particular Mathlib type/name, a separate object for every NL0
88: D node, or a duplicate formal representation. A mathematical source-to-code
89: identification can be checked semantically without constructing an unnecessary
90: second model. If the implementation actually crosses two different Lean
91: representations, the required conversion must occur in checked Lean code.
92: Unexplained equivalence, stronger assumptions, missing hypotheses, changed
93: domains or hidden target assumptions remain defects.
94: 
95: Do not accept an explanation on trust or copy the author's conclusion into the
96: review. Record PASS/FAIL/UNVERIFIED with specific findings and source/type/note
97: locations. A compiler pass cannot substitute for this independent judgment.
98: 
99: ## Freely available Mathlib
100: 
101: All proved results in the pinned Mathlib environment are available in stage
102: two. Do not compare their names, counts or node-by-node uses with the NL0 M
103: inventory. There is no per-M semantic row, imported-proof whitelist,
104: `calculation_links` ledger, or separate review of implementation N/D nodes.
105: Definitions are examined when they determine endpoint meaning, not for an
106: exact inventory match. Notes from Audit A are optional local guidance, not
107: permissions to use a library theorem.
108: 
109: New interfaces normally use Mathlib directly. An older or deliberately
110: conditional interface can retain M ports; `library_terms` supplies an actual
111: Lean proof for each such port at assembly. These are discharge proofs, not a
112: library correspondence inventory. They cannot remain unproved assumptions of
113: the final export. New external axioms or stronger project hypotheses still
114: require returning to the affected source boundary.
115: 
116: ## Mechanical evidence and limits
117: 
118: ### Compact review materials
119: 
120: The semantic reviewer reads the separately versioned
121: `yui-audit-b-review-view-1` in `review-packet.json`. Start at `/scope` and
122: `/mechanical_summary`, then examine each `/endpoints/<ID>` source, actual
123: inspected type and author correspondence. P retains the complete original
124: target, parameters and hypotheses. The view is a deterministic Python extraction,
125: not an LLM summary or mathematical judgment. It never substitutes a declared
126: expected type for the actual inspected type.
127: 
128: `/documents` identifies hash-bound `source-context.json`, `source-original.txt`
129: and actual `Proof.lean`. Read relevant original and Lean definitions there,
130: including hidden structure fields, when needed to interpret an endpoint.
131: Complete raw compiler, elaboration and dependency records stay in the machine
132: archive; they are not default reviewer inputs. A mechanical summary reports
133: actual checks and exceptions, without populating a semantic PASS. The full
134: dependency inspection remains a program responsibility.
135: 
136: Use `read_task_input` JSON pointers, not guessed fixed line positions. Large
137: containers expose keys and large strings expose `next_offset`. Text reads
138: resume with `next_start` and `next_column`. Serialized read results are at most
139: 32 KiB; follow `has_more` until the needed statement is complete. This pagination
140: limit is not a task time/token/call budget. Unknown calls or modified feedback
141: remain rejected with a specific local protocol fault, not a retryable HTTP 502.
142: 
143: ### Explicit reuse of completed native evidence
144: 
145: `audit_b.py reuse-review <new-directory> --original <old-audit-directory>`
146: prepares a new semantic review without rebuilding or changing Lean. It validates
147: every original input and snapshot, the original native artifacts/output, source
148: and accepted-A authority, environment pins, and the exact historical tool
149: snapshots. The new view and current reviewer runtime are separately bound in
150: `review-reuse.json`; the normal current-build tool check is not disabled.
151: Changed or incomplete evidence blocks reuse. Preserve the original failure.
152: 
153: The new independent reviewer receives no previous B verdict, reviewer history,
154: owner reasoning or other-case material. The receipt discloses inherited native
155: checks and a new semantic review; it cannot claim fresh compilation, an unaided
156: cold whole-workflow success or measured acceleration. Changing proofs or source
157: requires the appropriate new checks, rather than this review-only path.
158: 
159: `audit_b.py prepare/build/check` binds the source, accepted A, contract, plan,
160: proofs, tool versions and environment hashes. Build compiles standalone
161: `Proof.lean` before adding inspection. It checks E/P against their declared
162: encoded types, modulo definitional equality and bijective universe renaming.
163: It does not prove equivalence between natural-language text and Lean.
164: Distinct universes must not be collapsed; changed types or hypotheses must not
165: be normalized away. Source fidelity is established by the bound pre-proof independent review, or an actual exceptional B-final review; this native comparison does not establish it anew.
166: 
167: Inspection follows the actual `AuditBExport.P` closure. No `sorry`, unproved
168: local axiom/opaque substitute or undeclared foundation may be introduced.
169: Local bodies still compile against their own task inputs and the pinned
170: library; every required producer must exist. Assembly, inspection and semantic
171: review have separate recorded outcomes.
172: 
173: Version-1 receipts remain historical results under their original policy.
174: They cannot be silently relabeled or accepted as version-2 reviews. Start a
175: new bound audit when policy, source, code or evidence changes. Pending templates
176: never pass. A whole accepted source plus complete native gates and its bound semantic
177: authority yields `AUDIT-B-PASSED`; a fragment yields at most the explicitly
178: scoped development verdict. A whole source with an actual conditional Audit A
179: can yield `AUDIT-B-CONDITIONAL` after all the same native and semantic checks.
180: It retains the exact source warnings and never upgrades them to full PASS.
181: Neither proves external publications in Lean or
182: establishes formalizer speedup. Preserve failures and report actual costs.

1: # Irreducibility after reduction of an admissible sl2 lattice
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: James E. Humphreys, *Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory*,
6: Graduate Texts in Mathematics 9, Springer, section 27, exercise 7,
7: printed page 164. The exercise-list convention on page 163 sets
8: \(L=\mathfrak{sl}_2\) and identifies weights with integers.
9: Book DOI: [10.1007/978-1-4612-6398-2](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-6398-2).
10: 
11: > 7. If \(0\leq\lambda<\operatorname{char}K\), \(V=V(\lambda)\),
12: > prove that \(V(K)\) is irreducible as \(L(K)\)-module.
13: 
14: ## Definitions and complete target
15: 
16: Let \(p\) be any prime, \(K\) any field of characteristic \(p\), and
17: \(\lambda\) an integer with \(0\leq\lambda<p\).
18: Let \(V(\lambda)\) be the complex irreducible highest-weight
19: \(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)\)-module of highest weight \(\lambda\),
20: of dimension \(\lambda+1\). Its Chevalley generators satisfy
21: 
22: \[
23: [h,x]=2x,\qquad[h,y]=-2y,\qquad[x,y]=h.
24: \]
25: 
26: Choose a nonzero highest-weight vector \(v\) with \(xv=0\) and
27: \(hv=\lambda v\). Let \(U_{\mathbb Z}\) be the integer subalgebra of
28: the universal enveloping algebra generated by all divided powers
29: \(X_r=x^r/r!\), \(Y_r=y^r/r!\), for integers \(r\geq0\).
30: An **admissible lattice** \(M\subset V(\lambda)\) is a free abelian
31: subgroup with an integer basis that is also a complex basis, stable under
32: \(U_{\mathbb Z}\). It is arbitrary, not necessarily the minimal lattice.
33: 
34: Put \(V(K)=M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\). The Lie algebra
35: \(L(K)=(\mathbb Zx+\mathbb Zy+\mathbb Zh)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\)
36: acts by the induced lattice operators. This is the Chevalley
37: \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) construction also in characteristic 2.
38: Prove that \(V(K)\) is nonzero and every \(K\)-linear subspace
39: invariant under \(x,y,h\) is zero or all of \(V(K)\).

43: ## Fixed natural-language proof
44: 
45: ### 1. Divided-power coordinates in characteristic zero
46: 
47: Put \(n=\lambda+1\) and \(e_i=y^iv/i!\) for \(0\leq i\leq\lambda\).
48: The commutator identities give, by induction,
49: 
50: \[
51: hy^iv=(\lambda-2i)y^iv,\qquad
52: xy^iv=i(\lambda-i+1)y^{i-1}v\quad(i\geq1).
53: \]
54: 
55: For \(i\leq\lambda\), applying \(x^i\) to \(y^iv\) gives
56: \(i!\lambda(\lambda-1)\cdots(\lambda-i+1)v\ne0\) over \(\mathbb C\).
57: At \(i=0\) the empty product is one. Thus every \(e_i\ne0\).
58: Their \(h\)-eigenvalues \(\lambda-2i\) are distinct over \(\mathbb C\),
59: so they are linearly independent: applying
60: \(\prod_{k\ne j}(h-(\lambda-2k)\mathrm{Id})\) to a relation isolates
61: its \(j\)-th coefficient with a nonzero multiplier.
62: There are \(n\) vectors, the dimension of \(V(\lambda)\), hence they
63: form a basis. Also \(y^{\lambda+1}v=0\), since otherwise it would be
64: an eigenvector of eigenvalue \(-\lambda-2\), absent from this basis.
65: All higher lowering powers vanish as well.
66: 
67: The operator matrices are therefore
68: 
69: \[
70: xe_0=0,\quad xe_i=(\lambda-i+1)e_{i-1}\ (i\geq1),\qquad
71: ye_i=(i+1)e_{i+1}\ (i<\lambda),\quad ye_\lambda=0,
72: \quad he_i=(\lambda-2i)e_i.
73: \]
74: 
75: Iteration gives the integral divided-power matrices
76: 
77: \[
78: X_re_i=\binom{\lambda-i+r}{r}e_{i-r}\quad(0\leq r\leq i),
79: \qquad
80: Y_re_i=\binom{i+r}{r}e_{i+r}\quad(i+r\leq\lambda).       \tag{1}
81: \]
82: 
83: The respective expressions are zero when \(r>i\) or
84: \(i+r>\lambda\), by termination of the strings just proved.
85: 
86: ### 2. Matrix units preserve the localized arbitrary lattice
87: 
88: Let \(R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}=\{a/b\in\mathbb Q:p\nmid b\}\), and regard
89: \(M_R=R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M\) as a submodule of \(V(\lambda)\).
90: The embedding is injective because an integer basis of \(M\) is
91: complex-linearly independent. The module \(M_R\) is free of rank \(n\)
92: over \(R\) and is preserved by all \(X_r,Y_r\), by admissibility.
93: 
94: Define \(E_{ij}\) to send \(e_j\) to \(e_i\) and all other basis
95: vectors to zero. Formula (1) gives
96: 
97: \[
98: P:=Y_\lambda X_\lambda=E_{\lambda\lambda},\qquad
99: X_{\lambda-i}P=E_{i\lambda},\qquad
100: P Y_{\lambda-j}=\binom\lambda j E_{\lambda j}.
101: \]
102: 
103: For the last identity, an input index below \(j\) is sent below
104: \(e_\lambda\) and killed by \(P\); an index above \(j\) is sent past
105: the end of the lowering string. On \(e_j\) the coefficient is precisely
106: \(\binom\lambda j\). Since \(\lambda<p\), none of
107: \(\lambda!\), \(j!\), \((\lambda-j)!\) is divisible by \(p\), so
108: \(\binom\lambda j\) is a unit in \(R\). Consequently
109: 
110: \[
111: E_{ij}=\left(\binom\lambda j\right)^{-1}
112:        X_{\lambda-i}P Y_{\lambda-j}.                 \tag{2}
113: \]
114: 
115: Every matrix unit preserves \(M_R\). No assertion about distinct
116: weights modulo \(p\) has been used.
117: 
118: ### 3. Recover a standard basis for the arbitrary lattice
119: 
120: Define \(J_i=\{c\in\mathbb C:c e_i\in M_R\}\).
121: The coordinate projection \(E_{ii}\) maps \(M_R\) onto \(J_i e_i\).
122: Applying \(E_{ij}\) to \(c e_j\) shows \(J_j\subseteq J_i\);
123: reversing the indices gives equality. Let \(J\) be their common module.
124: It is finitely generated, being a projection of a finite free module,
125: and nonzero because \(M_R\) spans \(V(\lambda)\) over \(\mathbb C\).
126: The coordinate projections and independence of the \(e_i\) give
127: 
128: \[
129: M_R=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lambda}J e_i.                  \tag{3}
130: \]
131: 
132: One must still prove that \(J\) has rank one; containment in
133: \(\mathbb C\) alone does not imply that. Let
134: \(r=\dim_{\mathbb Q}(\mathbb Q\otimes_R J)\), which is finite.
135: Tensoring (3) with the fraction field \(\mathbb Q\) and using the
136: rank \(n\) of \(M_R\) gives \(n=nr\), so \(r=1\), since \(n>0\).
137: The multiplication map \(\mathbb Q\otimes_R J\to\mathbb C\) is
138: injective: this tensor product is the localization of the torsion-free
139: module \(J\subset\mathbb C\), and a fraction mapping to zero has
140: zero numerator. Thus \(J\) spans a one-dimensional rational line.
141: 
142: Choose \(0\ne a\in J\) and write a finite set of nonzero generators
143: as \(q_1a,\ldots,q_ka\) with \(q_j\in\mathbb Q^\times\).
144: Each \(q_j=p^{\nu_j}u_j\) for \(\nu_j\in\mathbb Z\) and a unit
145: \(u_j\) of \(R\). Let \(\nu=\min_j\nu_j\). All generators belong
146: to \(p^\nu R a\), and a generator with minimal exponent generates
147: that whole module. Therefore \(J=Rb\) for a nonzero \(b\in J\).
148: By (3), \(b e_0,\ldots,b e_\lambda\) is an \(R\)-basis of \(M_R\).
149: 
150: ### 4. Reduce and extend scalars
151: 
152: All denominators in \(R\) are invertible in \(K\), so the integer map
153: extends to \(R\to K\). The natural tensor maps give
154: 
155: \[
156: M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\cong M_R\otimes_R K
157: \cong(M_R/pM_R)\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}K.
158: \]
159: 
160: For example the first map sends \(m\otimes c\) to
161: \((1\otimes m)\otimes c\); its inverse sends
162: \((r\otimes m)\otimes c\) to \(m\otimes\bar r c\).
163: The reduced images \(b_0,\ldots,b_\lambda\) of \(b e_i\) form a
164: \(K\)-basis, with exactly the matrices of step 1 reduced into \(K\).
165: The matrix-unit identities (2) persist on this basis.
166: 
167: For \(0\leq r\leq\lambda<p\), \(r!\ne0\) in \(K\), and the induced
168: \(X_r,Y_r\) equal \((r!)^{-1}x^r,(r!)^{-1}y^r\). Hence any
169: \(K\)-subspace invariant under \(x,y\) is invariant under every matrix
170: unit in (2).
171: 
172: ### 5. Conclude irreducibility
173: 
174: Let \(W\) be invariant. If it is nonzero, choose
175: \(0\ne w=\sum_i c_i b_i\in W\), and an index \(j\) with \(c_j\ne0\).
176: For every \(i\), \(E_{ij}w=c_jb_i\in W\). Division by \(c_j\)
177: gives \(b_i\in W\), so all basis vectors lie in \(W\) and
178: \(W=V(K)\). Since \(\dim_K V(K)=\lambda+1>0\), it is nonzero and
179: irreducible. If \(\lambda=0\), all relevant factorials and binomial
180: coefficients are one and the argument applies unchanged. For \(p=2\),
181: the allowed \(\lambda\) are zero and one; the proof still works
182: without requiring distinct reduced \(h\)-eigenvalues.

14: ## Definitions and complete target
15: 
16: Let \(p\) be any prime, \(K\) any field of characteristic \(p\), and
17: \(\lambda\) an integer with \(0\leq\lambda<p\).
18: Let \(V(\lambda)\) be the complex irreducible highest-weight
19: \(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)\)-module of highest weight \(\lambda\),
20: of dimension \(\lambda+1\). Its Chevalley generators satisfy
21: 
22: \[
23: [h,x]=2x,\qquad[h,y]=-2y,\qquad[x,y]=h.
24: \]
25: 
26: Choose a nonzero highest-weight vector \(v\) with \(xv=0\) and
27: \(hv=\lambda v\). Let \(U_{\mathbb Z}\) be the integer subalgebra of
28: the universal enveloping algebra generated by all divided powers
29: \(X_r=x^r/r!\), \(Y_r=y^r/r!\), for integers \(r\geq0\).
30: An **admissible lattice** \(M\subset V(\lambda)\) is a free abelian
31: subgroup with an integer basis that is also a complex basis, stable under
32: \(U_{\mathbb Z}\). It is arbitrary, not necessarily the minimal lattice.
33: 
34: Put \(V(K)=M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\). The Lie algebra
35: \(L(K)=(\mathbb Zx+\mathbb Zy+\mathbb Zh)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\)
36: acts by the induced lattice operators. This is the Chevalley
37: \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) construction also in characteristic 2.
38: Prove that \(V(K)\) is nonzero and every \(K\)-linear subspace
39: invariant under \(x,y,h\) is zero or all of \(V(K)\).
40: Both \(\lambda=0\) and \(p=2\) are included; \(K\) need not be
41: algebraically closed.
42: 
43: ## Fixed natural-language proof
44: 
45: ### 1. Divided-power coordinates in characteristic zero
46: 
47: Put \(n=\lambda+1\) and \(e_i=y^iv/i!\) for \(0\leq i\leq\lambda\).
48: The commutator identities give, by induction,
49: 
50: \[
51: hy^iv=(\lambda-2i)y^iv,\qquad
52: xy^iv=i(\lambda-i+1)y^{i-1}v\quad(i\geq1).
53: \]
54: 
55: For \(i\leq\lambda\), applying \(x^i\) to \(y^iv\) gives
56: \(i!\lambda(\lambda-1)\cdots(\lambda-i+1)v\ne0\) over \(\mathbb C\).
57: At \(i=0\) the empty product is one. Thus every \(e_i\ne0\).
58: Their \(h\)-eigenvalues \(\lambda-2i\) are distinct over \(\mathbb C\),
59: so they are linearly independent: applying
60: \(\prod_{k\ne j}(h-(\lambda-2k)\mathrm{Id})\) to a relation isolates
61: its \(j\)-th coefficient with a nonzero multiplier.
62: There are \(n\) vectors, the dimension of \(V(\lambda)\), hence they
63: form a basis. Also \(y^{\lambda+1}v=0\), since otherwise it would be
64: an eigenvector of eigenvalue \(-\lambda-2\), absent from this basis.
65: All higher lowering powers vanish as well.
66: 
67: The operator matrices are therefore
68: 
69: \[
70: xe_0=0,\quad xe_i=(\lambda-i+1)e_{i-1}\ (i\geq1),\qquad
71: ye_i=(i+1)e_{i+1}\ (i<\lambda),\quad ye_\lambda=0,
72: \quad he_i=(\lambda-2i)e_i.
73: \]
74: 
75: Iteration gives the integral divided-power matrices
76: 
77: \[
78: X_re_i=\binom{\lambda-i+r}{r}e_{i-r}\quad(0\leq r\leq i),
79: \qquad
80: Y_re_i=\binom{i+r}{r}e_{i+r}\quad(i+r\leq\lambda).       \tag{1}
81: \]
82: 
83: The respective expressions are zero when \(r>i\) or
84: \(i+r>\lambda\), by termination of the strings just proved.
85: 
86: ### 2. Matrix units preserve the localized arbitrary lattice
87: 
88: Let \(R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}=\{a/b\in\mathbb Q:p\nmid b\}\), and regard
89: \(M_R=R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M\) as a submodule of \(V(\lambda)\).
90: The embedding is injective because an integer basis of \(M\) is
91: complex-linearly independent. The module \(M_R\) is free of rank \(n\)
92: over \(R\) and is preserved by all \(X_r,Y_r\), by admissibility.
93: 
94: Define \(E_{ij}\) to send \(e_j\) to \(e_i\) and all other basis
95: vectors to zero. Formula (1) gives
96: 
97: \[
98: P:=Y_\lambda X_\lambda=E_{\lambda\lambda},\qquad
99: X_{\lambda-i}P=E_{i\lambda},\qquad
100: P Y_{\lambda-j}=\binom\lambda j E_{\lambda j}.
101: \]
102: 
103: For the last identity, an input index below \(j\) is sent below
104: \(e_\lambda\) and killed by \(P\); an index above \(j\) is sent past
105: the end of the lowering string. On \(e_j\) the coefficient is precisely
106: \(\binom\lambda j\). Since \(\lambda<p\), none of
107: \(\lambda!\), \(j!\), \((\lambda-j)!\) is divisible by \(p\), so
108: \(\binom\lambda j\) is a unit in \(R\). Consequently
109: 
110: \[
111: E_{ij}=\left(\binom\lambda j\right)^{-1}
112:        X_{\lambda-i}P Y_{\lambda-j}.                 \tag{2}
113: \]
114: 
115: Every matrix unit preserves \(M_R\). No assertion about distinct
116: weights modulo \(p\) has been used.
117: 
118: ### 3. Recover a standard basis for the arbitrary lattice
119: 
120: Define \(J_i=\{c\in\mathbb C:c e_i\in M_R\}\).
121: The coordinate projection \(E_{ii}\) maps \(M_R\) onto \(J_i e_i\).
122: Applying \(E_{ij}\) to \(c e_j\) shows \(J_j\subseteq J_i\);
123: reversing the indices gives equality. Let \(J\) be their common module.
124: It is finitely generated, being a projection of a finite free module,
125: and nonzero because \(M_R\) spans \(V(\lambda)\) over \(\mathbb C\).
126: The coordinate projections and independence of the \(e_i\) give
127: 
128: \[
129: M_R=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lambda}J e_i.                  \tag{3}
130: \]
131: 
132: One must still prove that \(J\) has rank one; containment in
133: \(\mathbb C\) alone does not imply that. Let
134: \(r=\dim_{\mathbb Q}(\mathbb Q\otimes_R J)\), which is finite.
135: Tensoring (3) with the fraction field \(\mathbb Q\) and using the
136: rank \(n\) of \(M_R\) gives \(n=nr\), so \(r=1\), since \(n>0\).
137: The multiplication map \(\mathbb Q\otimes_R J\to\mathbb C\) is

138: injective: this tensor product is the localization of the torsion-free
139: module \(J\subset\mathbb C\), and a fraction mapping to zero has
140: zero numerator. Thus \(J\) spans a one-dimensional rational line.
141: 
142: Choose \(0\ne a\in J\) and write a finite set of nonzero generators
143: as \(q_1a,\ldots,q_ka\) with \(q_j\in\mathbb Q^\times\).
144: Each \(q_j=p^{\nu_j}u_j\) for \(\nu_j\in\mathbb Z\) and a unit
145: \(u_j\) of \(R\). Let \(\nu=\min_j\nu_j\). All generators belong
146: to \(p^\nu R a\), and a generator with minimal exponent generates
147: that whole module. Therefore \(J=Rb\) for a nonzero \(b\in J\).
148: By (3), \(b e_0,\ldots,b e_\lambda\) is an \(R\)-basis of \(M_R\).
149: 
150: ### 4. Reduce and extend scalars
151: 
152: All denominators in \(R\) are invertible in \(K\), so the integer map
153: extends to \(R\to K\). The natural tensor maps give
154: 
155: \[
156: M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\cong M_R\otimes_R K
157: \cong(M_R/pM_R)\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}K.
158: \]
159: 
160: For example the first map sends \(m\otimes c\) to
161: \((1\otimes m)\otimes c\); its inverse sends
162: \((r\otimes m)\otimes c\) to \(m\otimes\bar r c\).
163: The reduced images \(b_0,\ldots,b_\lambda\) of \(b e_i\) form a
164: \(K\)-basis, with exactly the matrices of step 1 reduced into \(K\).
165: The matrix-unit identities (2) persist on this basis.
166: 
167: For \(0\leq r\leq\lambda<p\), \(r!\ne0\) in \(K\), and the induced
168: \(X_r,Y_r\) equal \((r!)^{-1}x^r,(r!)^{-1}y^r\). Hence any
169: \(K\)-subspace invariant under \(x,y\) is invariant under every matrix
170: unit in (2).
171: 
172: ### 5. Conclude irreducibility
173: 
174: Let \(W\) be invariant. If it is nonzero, choose
175: \(0\ne w=\sum_i c_i b_i\in W\), and an index \(j\) with \(c_j\ne0\).
176: For every \(i\), \(E_{ij}w=c_jb_i\in W\). Division by \(c_j\)
177: gives \(b_i\in W\), so all basis vectors lie in \(W\) and
178: \(W=V(K)\). Since \(\dim_K V(K)=\lambda+1>0\), it is nonzero and
179: irreducible. If \(\lambda=0\), all relevant factorials and binomial
180: coefficients are one and the argument applies unchanged. For \(p=2\),
181: the allowed \(\lambda\) are zero and one; the proof still works
182: without requiring distinct reduced \(h\)-eigenvalues.
183:

R001.fact: For every natural m, m! is a positive integer and its image in C is nonzero. A finite product of positive integers likewise has nonzero image in C, including the empty product 1. Hence all factorial divisions and cancellations in D003,D004,D009 and S003,S007 are legitimate.

grounds.reason: V is a complex vector space, so the scalar field for these operations is C.
The divided-power index r is natural.
The divided-power index r is natural.
The basis-family index i is natural and finite.
For 1<=r<=i<=ell, both r and ell-r+1 are positive integers.
All factorial arguments are natural, with ell-i>=0 and the stated endpoint guards.

R001.justification: Induction using 0!=1 and (m+1)!=(m+1)m! gives positivity. The usual integer embedding into C is injective (C has characteristic zero), so positive integers remain nonzero. The field has no zero divisors, and the inverse of a nonzero scalar allows the displayed divisions and cancellations.

R002.fact: For every natural r, r! is a positive natural integer, hence its images in Z and C are nonzero. Thus (r!:C)(r!:C)^(-1)=1, and multiplication by a product of factorials can be cancelled in Z or C.

grounds.reason: D003 defines X_r using the complex inverse of r! for natural r.
D004 defines Y_r with the same natural factorial denominator.

R002.justification: The empty factorial product is 1; every factor of any nonempty factorial is a positive integer. Their finite product is positive. The standard embeddings Z→C and N→Z preserve these nonzero integers, and cancellation follows in the integral domain Z and field C.

R002.fact: For a complex basis (e_k) indexed by Fin(n), prescribing images w_k in V defines a unique complex-linear endomorphism T of V with T(e_k)=w_k. In particular the prescription w_k=e_i if k=j and 0 otherwise defines E_ij.

grounds.reason: N001 states that (e_k) indexed by Fin(n) is a complex basis of V.
The prescribed images lie in V and the indices i,j,k lie in Fin(n).

R002.justification: Every vector has a unique finite basis expansion sum_k a_k e_k. Set T(sum_k a_k e_k)=sum_k a_k w_k. Uniqueness of coordinates makes this well-defined; addition and scalar multiplication of coordinates prove complex linearity. The same expansion proves uniqueness.

R002.fact: For a Z-submodule M of V with injective inclusion iota, restrictions of ambient linear operators preserving M intertwine with iota. Restriction respects composition, integer scalar multiples, finite sums and identity. Hence an ambient equality built from these operations implies the corresponding equality in End_Z(M).

grounds.reason: M is the stated Z-submodule and is stable under the divided-power-generated U_Z.
S001 establishes preservation by X_r,Y_r and the injective inclusion.
D016 defines Q_M as the product of the appropriate restrictions.
D017 defines A_ij as a product of those restrictions.
F005 establishes the ambient product and finite diagonal-sum identities with integer coefficients.

R002.justification: For m in M, applying inclusion to a restricted operator gives the ambient operator applied to iota(m). Repeated substitution proves the same statement for compositions, sums and integer multiples, using additivity of inclusion. After applying an ambient identity at iota(m), injectivity gives the desired equality at m. Pointwise equality gives equality of endomorphisms; no preservation by the unscaled coordinate operators is required.

R003.fact: Every field L satisfies the strong rank condition: an injective L-linear map L^r to L^s for finite natural r,s implies r<=s. In particular this holds for C in S001 and K in S002.

grounds.reason: V is a vector space over the standard field C; M009 is applied over C.
K is explicitly a field; M005 is applied over K.

R003.justification: The images of the r standard basis vectors under an injective map are linearly independent in L^s. Gaussian elimination of the s-by-r matrix uses field division by nonzero pivots and gives at most s pivot columns. Independence requires all r columns to be pivot columns, so r<=s. This verifies the strong rank premises without assuming any target dimension formula.

R003.fact: A finite-dimensional vector space is finitely generated as a module over its field. A finite set I of cardinality n admits a bijection Fin(n) to I.

grounds.reason: lambda is nonnegative, identifying it with ell.
The ordinary complex dimension of V is the finite integer lambda+1.
M008 makes I finite and M009 identifies its natural cardinality with n before the bijection is chosen.

R003.justification: Finite dimension means a finite basis exists, and that basis is a finite spanning set, which is exactly finite generation. A finite set of cardinality n can be enumerated by its n distinct elements, giving the stated bijection. Thus the chosen beta depends on an established finite cardinality, not on an unsupported choice of lattice basis.

R003.fact: If b:I to M is an R-basis and beta:J to I is a bijection, then j maps to b(beta(j)) is an R-basis. Over a nonzero field every vector of a basis is nonzero.

grounds.reason: H007 provides bZ as an integer basis with the corresponding complex basis.
F001 provides the finite-cardinality bijection used for beta.
qBasis is the canonical K-basis supplied by base change, indexed by Fin(n), and n=ell+1 is positive.

R003.justification: Under a bijection, finite coordinate families are reindexed bijectively; spanning expansions and uniqueness of coefficients are preserved. If a basis vector were zero, the finite coefficient family with coefficient 1 at its index and 0 elsewhere would represent zero, contradicting uniqueness against the all-zero family. K is a field, so 1 differs from 0.

R003.fact: For an algebraic tensor product over Z, a biadditive Z-balanced rule into an abelian group extends uniquely to an additive map. Two additive maps agreeing on every pure tensor agree everywhere. For a fixed scalar, equality expressing K-linearity can likewise be checked on pure tensors when both sides are additive.

grounds.reason: The tensor products are algebraic, generated additively by pure tensors with additivity and Z-balancing relations.
U uses the corresponding first-factor K-action.
The formula for F(f) is biadditive and balanced because f is Z-linear.

R003.justification: Present the tensor product as the free abelian group on pairs modulo the biadditivity and balancing relations. Any rule satisfying those relations descends to the quotient. Every element is a finite integer combination of generators; integer coefficients can be absorbed into a tensor factor. Additivity therefore extends equality from pure tensors to all elements. Multiplication by a fixed K scalar is additive, so equality of the two additive maps in a scalar-compatibility identity can also be tested on generators. The later applications must, and do, check their particular formulas; the background fact itself uses only the supplied algebraic tensor-product definitions.

R003.fact: If S:A to B is a linear isomorphism, T:A to A and Q:B to B are linear, and ST=QS, then W maps to S(W) is a bijection between T-invariant subspaces of A and Q-invariant subspaces of B, with inverse Z maps to S_inv(Z). It sends zero and whole spaces to zero and whole spaces.

F(f) is a K-linear operator on U.
ind(f) is a K-linear operator on V_K.
For arbitrary f0, the displayed pure-tensor calculation proves S ind(f0)=F(f0) S everywhere.

R003.justification: The image of a subspace under a linear map is a subspace. If T(W) is contained in W, then Q(S(W))=S(T(W)) is contained in S(W). From ST=QS and the inverse identities one obtains T S_inv=S_inv Q, proving the converse for inverse images. The mutually inverse maps S and S_inv make these subspace assignments inverse bijections. Linearity sends zero to zero and surjectivity sends A onto B.

R004.fact: For the supplied unital ring homomorphism F:End_Z(M)→End_K(U), every integer t and f∈End_Z(M) satisfy F(t·f)=red(t)·F(f). For K-linear endomorphisms P,Q and scalars a,b∈K, (a·P)(b·Q)=(ab)·(PQ).

red is the canonical integer map into K.

R004.justification: For nonnegative t, additivity gives F(t·f)=t·F(f) by finite induction; preservation of negation extends this to integers. In End_K(U), this repeated integer addition equals multiplication by red(t), as seen on each vector. Also P(bQ(u))=bP(Q(u)) by K-linearity, so evaluation gives (aP)(bQ)(u)=ab(PQ)(u). These facts justify the scalar transfers and rearrangements used in S002 and again in S003.

R004.fact: For a K-linear subspace W of U, if P preserves W then P^s preserves W for every natural s. If P and Q preserve W, then PQ preserves W, and aP preserves W for every a∈K.

grounds.reason: W is an arbitrary K-linear subspace of U.
L2 assumes stability under F(x_M) and F(y_M); F003 supplies scalar-power formulas before they are used.
Stability means that each vector of W is mapped into W.
The divided-power formulas hold for all indices at most ell.

R004.justification: The identity preserves W. Inductively, P^(s+1)(w)=P(P^s(w)) lies in W. Similarly, PQ(w) lies in W by applying Q and then P, and aP(w) lies in W by closure of a K-subspace under scalar multiplication. Applying these facts to F003 and to the four factors displayed in S004 verifies precisely the stated stability step.

R005.fact: For a vector u≠0 in a vector space over a field k, a·u=0 implies a=0. For a finite index type I, a family b:I→U is linearly independent precisely when every relation ∑_{i∈I} a_i·b_i=0 has all a_i=0.

argument.text: H005 gives hy=yh−2y and xy=yx+h. Prove h y^i v=(ell−2i)y^i v for every i≥0 by induction: the base is F001; for the step fix t and temporarily assume L1: h y^t v=(ell−2t)y^t v. Then h y^(t+1)v=(yh−2y)y^t v=(ell−2t−2)y^(t+1)v. Discharge L1 to the induction step. For the second identity the base is xyv=yxv+hv=ell v. In the step t≥1, assume L2: xy^t v=t(ell−t+1)y^(t−1)v. Then xy^(t+1)v=y(xy^t v)+hy^t v=[t(ell−t+1)+(ell−2t)]y^t v=(t+1)(ell−t)y^t v. Discharge L2; induction gives xy^i v=i(ell−i+1)y^(i−1)v for every i≥1. These identities do not assume termination.

argument.text: For each 0≤i≤ell, repeated use of F002 gives x^i y^i v=[∏_{r=1}^i r(ell−r+1)]v. For i>0 all displayed factors are positive integers; for i=0 the product is 1. In C they are nonzero, so v≠0 forces y^i v≠0. Since i!≠0, e_i≠0. F002 also gives he_i=(ell−2i)e_i. The eigenvalues are pairwise distinct: ell−2i=ell−2j in C implies 2(i−j)=0 and hence i=j in characteristic zero.

argument.text: Take arbitrary coefficients zeta and temporarily assume L3: ∑_i zeta_i e_i=0. Fix j∈Fin(n) and apply ∏_{k≠j}(h−(ell−2k)Id). The factors commute because each is a polynomial in h. Every term of index i≠j is killed by its factor k=i; the surviving term is zeta_j[∏_{k≠j}((ell−2j)−(ell−2k))]e_j=0. By F003 the product and e_j are nonzero, including the empty product. Thus zeta_j=0. This holds for every j. Discharging L3 proves complex linear independence of e.

argument.text: Apply M001 with division ring C, vector space V, index set Fin(n), and family e. Fin(n) has n elements, V is finite-dimensional of dimension n by F001, and F004 supplies independence. The span is V. Together with independence this makes e a basis.

argument.text: Put zvec=y^(ell+1)v and alpha_i its e-basis coordinates. M006 with this basis expands zvec=∑_i alpha_i e_i. F002 gives h zvec=(−ell−2)zvec, and applying h−(−ell−2)Id to this expansion gives ∑_i alpha_i[2(ell+1−i)]e_i=0. For every i≤ell the bracketed integer is positive, hence nonzero in C. Independence F004 forces every alpha_i=0, so zvec=0. Applying further powers of y gives y^s v=0 for all s≥ell+1.

argument.text: Divide the recurrences F002 by i!, using (i+1)!=(i+1)i!, and combine F006 at the top endpoint. This gives xe_0=0, xe_i=(ell−i+1)e_(i−1) for i≥1, ye_i=(i+1)e_(i+1) for i<ell, ye_ell=0 and he_i=(ell−2i)e_i. For r≤i, iteration of x yields ∏_{s=1}^r(ell−i+s) on e_(i−r). After division by r!, M004 at (n0,j0)=(ell−i+r,r), and cancellation of (ell−i)!≠0 in C, gives choose(ell−i+r,r). If r>i the string reaches e_0 and is killed. For i+r≤ell, iteration of y yields (i+r)!/i! on e_(i+r); division by r!, using M004 at (i+r,r), gives choose(i+r,r). If i+r>ell the string reaches e_ell and is killed by y. Thus both zero cases and r=0 are included. These formulas together with F001,F005,F006 prove the full coordinate and termination statement.

To record how operator equalities will be checked, fix arbitrary complex endomorphisms fop,gop and temporarily assume L1 that they agree on each e_i. argument.text: Put Q_C=Y_ell X_ell. The N001 divided-power formulas show X_ell kills e_k for k<ell and sends e_ell to e_0, while Y_ell e_0=e_ell. Thus Q_C=E_(ell,ell), by F002. They also give X_(ell−i)e_ell=e_i (its binomial coefficient is choose(ell−i,ell−i)=1), so X_(ell−i)Q_C=E_(i,ell) for every i. All formulas include ell=0.

argument.text: Put A_C_ij=X_(ell−i)Q_C Y_(ell−j). On e_k, if k<j the vector Y_(ell−j)e_k has index below ell and is killed by Q_C; if k>j it goes past the top index and is already zero. For k=j it is choose(ell,ell−j)e_ell. M004 at (ell,j) and (ell,ell−j) gives choose(ell,j) j!(ell−j)!=ell!=choose(ell,ell−j)(ell−j)!j!. Cancel the nonzero integer factorial product to obtain choose(ell,ell−j)=choose(ell,j)=c_j. Hence Q_C Y_(ell−j)=c_j E_(ell,j), and F003 gives A_C_ij=c_j E_ij. In each instance equality on every basis vector is promoted to equality of endomorphisms by F002.

argument.text: On every basis vector, E_ij E_kl equals E_il if j=k and 0 otherwise; F002 proves the operator identity. By F004, A_C_ij A_C_kl=c_j A_C_il if j=k (both sides are c_j c_l E_il), and 0 otherwise. By definition d_j c_j=Dprod, also for the singleton index set. Acting on e_k gives (∑_j d_j A_C_jj)e_k=Dprod e_k. F002 therefore gives ∑_j d_j A_C_jj=Dprod Id_V.

argument.text: The products defining Q_M,A_ij are restrictions of Q_C,A_C_ij, since all their divided-power factors preserve M. Along with d_j c_j=Dprod and F001 this proves the full integral-operator statement. Only c_j E_ij is asserted to preserve M over Z.

argument.text: The K,M,F names in E001's verbatim source statement are source-bound (their ledger aliases are k0,M0,G0). For each f, both G(f) and F(f) are additive maps, and every tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors, so they agree everywhere. argument.text: H003 gives lambda=(ell:Z) and ell<p. Since p is prime and char K=p (H001,H002), M003 at r0=ell gives that red(ell!) is a unit, hence nonzero in the field K. For j∈Fin(n), M004 at (ell,j) gives c_j j!(ell−j)!=ell!. After applying red this is red(c_j) red(j!) red((ell−j)!)=red(ell!)≠0. No factor of a nonzero product in a field can be zero, so red(c_j)≠0 for every j. The finite product red(Dprod)=∏_j red(c_j) is nonzero.

argument.text: Use the ring-homomorphism laws of F from N003 on N002. Integer multiples of an endomorphism become scalar multiples by their image in K: repeated addition and negation commute with F. Scalars commute with K-linear maps. When j≠k, the integer multiplication identity gives T_ij T_k,lidx=0. When j=k it gives T_ij T_j,lidx=red(c_j)^(-1)red(c_lidx)^(-1)F(c_j A_i,lidx)=red(c_lidx)^(-1)F(A_i,lidx)=T_i,lidx. Cancellation uses F001. The sum identity becomes ∑_j red(d_j)F(A_jj)=red(Dprod)Id_U. From d_j c_j=Dprod and F001, red(d_j)=red(Dprod)red(c_j)^(-1); divide the sum identity by the nonzero red(Dprod) to get ∑_j T_jj=Id_U. These are endomorphism identities on U; no reduction of the characteristic-zero e-basis has been presumed.

argument.text: Choose j0 from F002 and put u0=T0_j0,j0(w0). Stability gives u0∈W0; it is nonzero by choice. The relation T0_j0,j0^2=T0_j0,j0 gives T0_j0,j0(u0)=u0. Define uFamily_i=T0_i,j0(u0). Every uFamily_i belongs to W0 by stability.

argument.text: Take arbitrary coefficients acoef and assume L4: ∑_i acoef_i uFamily_i=0. Fix kidx∈Fin(n0) and apply T0_j0,kidx. The multiplication law from L1 kills every term except i=kidx, yielding 0=∑_i acoef_i T0_j0,kidx T0_i,j0(u0)=acoef_kidx T0_j0,j0(u0)=acoef_kidx u0. Since k0 is a field and u0≠0 by F003, acoef_kidx=0. argument.text: Apply M001 to the field k0 (a division ring), the finite-dimensional U0, Fin(n0), and uFamily. L1 gives dim U0=n0 and F004 gives independence, so this family's span is U0. F003 says every family vector is in W0, so closure under linear combinations gives W0=U0 in the nonzero branch. Discharge L2 and combine it with the zero branch of S002, obtaining W0={0} or W0=U0. Discharge L1 to the full implication, and universally quantify all the originally arbitrary data. This proves the asserted general irreducibility lemma, even if n0 has zero image in k0: there was no division by n0 or trace calculation.

argument.text: H007 and N002 identify x_M,y_M,h_M with the integral restrictions of the stipulated x,y,h. Their integer Chevalley relations follow from H005 by applying the injective inclusion M→V: [h_M,x_M]=2x_M, [h_M,y_M]=−2y_M and [x_M,y_M]=h_M. By N003, scalar extension F preserves these identities, and S intertwines F with each induced operator ind on V_K. Thus the original induced x,y,h actions are exactly ind(x_M),ind(y_M),ind(h_M), with the stipulated Chevalley relations after tensoring over Z. This is valid in characteristic 2 as well: the L_K=L_Z⊗_Z K action is the K-linear extension of the integral action of the three formal Chevalley generators. Invariance under the three generators is equivalent to invariance under every K-linear combination of them. N003 already gives V_K≠0.

Let W be any K-linear subspace of V_K, and assume L1: W is invariant under the induced x,y,h operators. Put Zsub=S(W). By N003 it is a K-linear subspace of U; the intertwining formulas and L1 make it invariant under F(x_M),F(y_M). N004 therefore makes it invariant under all T_ij and supplies the multiplication and diagonal-sum relations. N003 gives dim_K U=n=ell+1>0. Apply N005 at field K, size n, space U, family T and subspace Zsub: Zsub={0} or Zsub=U. Apply S_inv, using the inverse identities in N003, to obtain W={0} or W=V_K. Discharge L1 and quantify W. Together with nonzeroness from N003 this proves P.

For the endpoints, H003 gives ell<p, H001 gives p prime, and H002 gives char K=p. If lambda=0 then ell=0,n=1, X_0=Y_0=Id, c_0=Dprod=d_0=1, and all the same formulas apply. If p=2 then ell∈{0,1}; every factorial inverted in the stability argument has index at most ell<2. The e-basis in N001 lives in V over C; none of the reduced matrix-unit premises used in S002 requires distinct h-eigenvalues in K. No step imposed algebraic closure of K or a minimal-lattice condition. Thus the conclusion covers the complete original parameter range.

value.N002: For every natural r, r!·X_M(r)=x_M^r and r!·Y_M(r)=y_M^r in End_Z(M). The inclusion M→V intertwines x_M,y_M,h_M with x,y,h respectively; in particular h preserves M. For all i,j,k,l∈Fin(n), A_ij A_kl=c_j·A_il if j=k, and 0 otherwise. With Dprod=∏_j c_j and d_j=∏_{k≠j}c_k one has d_j c_j=Dprod and ∑_j d_j·A_jj=Dprod·Id_M.
value.N003: U has a K-basis of length n=ell+1, dim_K U=n>0, and U≠0. The function F is a unital ring homomorphism End_Z(M)→End_K(U), with F(f)(a⊗m)=a⊗f(m). The map S:V_K→U is K-linear, has inverse S_inv, and hence is a K-linear isomorphism. V_K≠0. For every f∈End_Z(M), S∘ind(f)=F(f)∘S. Consequently S transports invariant subspaces for any such pair of operators bijectively, and transports zero and whole spaces to zero and whole spaces.
value.N004: For every j∈Fin(n), red(c_j)≠0 and red(Dprod)≠0. For i,j,k,l∈Fin(n), T_ij T_kl=T_il if j=k and 0 otherwise, and ∑_j T_jj=Id_U. For every K-linear subspace W of U, if W is invariant under F(x_M) and F(y_M), then W is invariant under every T_ij. Moreover ell<p, and for every natural r≤ell one has red(r!)≠0, F(X_M(r))=red(r!)^(-1)F(x_M)^r and F(Y_M(r))=red(r!)^(-1)F(y_M)^r.
value.N005: For every field k0, positive natural n0, k0-vector space U0 of dimension n0, and family T0_ij∈End_{k0}(U0), i,j∈Fin(n0), if for all i,j,k,l∈Fin(n0), T0_ij T0_kl equals T0_il when j=k and 0 otherwise, and ∑_j T0_jj=Id_{U0}, then every k0-linear subspace W0 invariant under all T0_ij satisfies W0={0} or W0=U0.

value.statement:
Let \(p\) be any prime, \(K\) any field of characteristic \(p\), and
\(\lambda\) an integer with \(0\leq\lambda<p\).
Let \(V(\lambda)\) be the complex irreducible highest-weight
\(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)\)-module of highest weight \(\lambda\),
of dimension \(\lambda+1\). Its Chevalley generators satisfy

\[
[h,x]=2x,\qquad[h,y]=-2y,\qquad[x,y]=h.
\]

Choose a nonzero highest-weight vector \(v\) with \(xv=0\) and
\(hv=\lambda v\). Let \(U_{\mathbb Z}\) be the integer subalgebra of
the universal enveloping algebra generated by all divided powers
\(X_r=x^r/r!\), \(Y_r=y^r/r!\), for integers \(r\geq0\).
An **admissible lattice** \(M\subset V(\lambda)\) is a free abelian
subgroup with an integer basis that is also a complex basis, stable under
\(U_{\mathbb Z}\). It is arbitrary, not necessarily the minimal lattice.

Put \(V(K)=M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\). The Lie algebra
\(L(K)=(\mathbb Zx+\mathbb Zy+\mathbb Zh)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\)
acts by the induced lattice operators. This is the Chevalley
\(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) construction also in characteristic 2.
Prove that \(V(K)\) is nonzero and every \(K\)-linear subspace
invariant under \(x,y,h\) is zero or all of \(V(K)\).
Both \(\lambda=0\) and \(p=2\) are included; \(K\) need not be
algebraically closed.

Transfer any invariant subspace through the intertwining tensor swap B104, apply B103 and B105, and transfer back. B104 supplies nonzeroness. The p=2 and lambda=0 cases are covered by the same formulas.

import Mathlib

namespace YuiBasisObjects

noncomputable def dividedPower {V : Type*} [AddCommGroup V] [Module ℂ V]
    (f : Module.End ℂ V) (r : ℕ) : Module.End ℂ V :=
  ((r.factorial : ℂ)⁻¹) • f ^ r

def Stable {K V : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V]
    (W : Submodule K V) (f : Module.End K V) : Prop :=
  ∀ w, w ∈ W → f w ∈ W

structure AdmissibleLattice (n : ℕ) (V : Type*) [AddCommGroup V] [Module ℂ V]
    (x y : Module.End ℂ V) where
  carrier : Submodule ℤ V
  zBasis : Module.Basis (Fin n) ℤ carrier
  cBasis : Module.Basis (Fin n) ℂ V
  coe_basis : ∀ i, (zBasis i : V) = cBasis i
  stableX : ∀ (r : ℕ) (m : V), m ∈ carrier → dividedPower x r m ∈ carrier
  stableY : ∀ (r : ℕ) (m : V), m ∈ carrier → dividedPower y r m ∈ carrier

end YuiBasisObjects

1: # Lean implementation safeguards
2: 
3: Apply these requirements within the accepted NL0 and the fixed Lean interface.
4: They govern implementation, not additional NL0 detail or a weaker Audit B.
5: Use existing library readers and local checking tools; no separate review
6: model, new premise or mandatory lookup of every familiar declaration is needed.
7: 
8: 1. **Check critical library signatures.** Before relying on a critical or
9:    unfamiliar library application, establish its complete type in the pinned
10:    environment, including explicit, implicit and instance binders and all
11:    side conditions. Read the declaration or check a small typed application
12:    when its signature is uncertain. Do not infer the calling convention from
13:    its name or pass an implicit argument as though it were an explicit one.
14:    A previously checked signature in this context need not be looked up again.
15: 2. **Constrain difficult inference.** When coercions or implicit inference
16:    obscure the intended application, give the intermediate fact an explicit
17:    type and supply the relevant named parameters, such as the set, exponent
18:    or ambient space. Prefer this to leaving Lean to discover those choices by
19:    unfolding large definitions. Routine unambiguous arguments can stay
20:    implicit; explicit parameters must preserve the existing target and inputs.
21: 3. **Check conversions before combining them.** When an argument crosses Lean
22:    representations, first establish a small typed conversion fact, then use
23:    it in the main proof. In particular, distinguish `ℝ`, `ℝ≥0` and `ℝ≥0∞`;
24:    check the conversion direction, nonnegativity and any finiteness conditions.
25:    A conversion is not automatically invertible, and matching notation does
26:    not establish equality of differently typed expressions. Reuse a checked
27:    fact when available. Do not invent another representation, a global helper
28:    requirement or an extra hypothesis just to satisfy this instruction.
29: 4. **Isolate an inference failure.** If compiler feedback identifies a library
30:    application, coercion or expensive inference problem, reduce the next check
31:    to that application or conversion with explicit local types before adding
32:    more proof code. Use `check_auxiliary` in a proof worker, or
33:    `check_lean_types` during preparation when that tool is supplied. Helpers
34:    use only the current allowed inputs and never become new premises. Once
35:    the small check succeeds, integrate the result and recheck the complete
36:    obligation; success of a helper alone does not accept the target.
37: 
38: 5. **Repair after a bounded check.** Native checks have a separate per-call wall
39:    limit, normally 180 seconds, and use the controller-owned 20,000,000 heartbeat budget.
40:    A timeout or heartbeat diagnostic leaves the goal unaccepted and returns
41:    control to the same worker. Inspect the retained candidate and diagnostic,
42:    then check a smaller typed application, conversion or proof fragment before
43:    integrating it. Do not repeat the unchanged expensive candidate or disable

R001.fact: For every natural m, m! is a positive integer and its image in C is nonzero. A finite product of positive integers likewise has nonzero image in C, including the empty product 1. Hence all factorial divisions and cancellations in D003,D004,D009 and S003,S007 are legitimate.

grounds.reason: V is a complex vector space, so the scalar field for these operations is C.
The divided-power index r is natural.
The divided-power index r is natural.
The basis-family index i is natural and finite.
For 1<=r<=i<=ell, both r and ell-r+1 are positive integers.
All factorial arguments are natural, with ell-i>=0 and the stated endpoint guards.

R001.justification: Induction using 0!=1 and (m+1)!=(m+1)m! gives positivity. The usual integer embedding into C is injective (C has characteristic zero), so positive integers remain nonzero. The field has no zero divisors, and the inverse of a nonzero scalar allows the displayed divisions and cancellations.

R002.fact: For every natural r, r! is a positive natural integer, hence its images in Z and C are nonzero. Thus (r!:C)(r!:C)^(-1)=1, and multiplication by a product of factorials can be cancelled in Z or C.

grounds.reason: D003 defines X_r using the complex inverse of r! for natural r.
D004 defines Y_r with the same natural factorial denominator.

R002.justification: The empty factorial product is 1; every factor of any nonempty factorial is a positive integer. Their finite product is positive. The standard embeddings Z→C and N→Z preserve these nonzero integers, and cancellation follows in the integral domain Z and field C.

R002.fact: For a complex basis (e_k) indexed by Fin(n), prescribing images w_k in V defines a unique complex-linear endomorphism T of V with T(e_k)=w_k. In particular the prescription w_k=e_i if k=j and 0 otherwise defines E_ij.

grounds.reason: N001 states that (e_k) indexed by Fin(n) is a complex basis of V.
The prescribed images lie in V and the indices i,j,k lie in Fin(n).

R002.justification: Every vector has a unique finite basis expansion sum_k a_k e_k. Set T(sum_k a_k e_k)=sum_k a_k w_k. Uniqueness of coordinates makes this well-defined; addition and scalar multiplication of coordinates prove complex linearity. The same expansion proves uniqueness.

R002.fact: For a Z-submodule M of V with injective inclusion iota, restrictions of ambient linear operators preserving M intertwine with iota. Restriction respects composition, integer scalar multiples, finite sums and identity. Hence an ambient equality built from these operations implies the corresponding equality in End_Z(M).

grounds.reason: M is the stated Z-submodule and is stable under the divided-power-generated U_Z.
S001 establishes preservation by X_r,Y_r and the injective inclusion.
D016 defines Q_M as the product of the appropriate restrictions.
D017 defines A_ij as a product of those restrictions.
F005 establishes the ambient product and finite diagonal-sum identities with integer coefficients.

R002.justification: For m in M, applying inclusion to a restricted operator gives the ambient operator applied to iota(m). Repeated substitution proves the same statement for compositions, sums and integer multiples, using additivity of inclusion. After applying an ambient identity at iota(m), injectivity gives the desired equality at m. Pointwise equality gives equality of endomorphisms; no preservation by the unscaled coordinate operators is required.

R003.fact: Every field L satisfies the strong rank condition: an injective L-linear map L^r to L^s for finite natural r,s implies r<=s. In particular this holds for C in S001 and K in S002.

grounds.reason: V is a vector space over the standard field C; M009 is applied over C.
K is explicitly a field; M005 is applied over K.

R003.justification: The images of the r standard basis vectors under an injective map are linearly independent in L^s. Gaussian elimination of the s-by-r matrix uses field division by nonzero pivots and gives at most s pivot columns. Independence requires all r columns to be pivot columns, so r<=s. This verifies the strong rank premises without assuming any target dimension formula.

R003.fact: A finite-dimensional vector space is finitely generated as a module over its field. A finite set I of cardinality n admits a bijection Fin(n) to I.

grounds.reason: lambda is nonnegative, identifying it with ell.
The ordinary complex dimension of V is the finite integer lambda+1.
M008 makes I finite and M009 identifies its natural cardinality with n before the bijection is chosen.

R003.justification: Finite dimension means a finite basis exists, and that basis is a finite spanning set, which is exactly finite generation. A finite set of cardinality n can be enumerated by its n distinct elements, giving the stated bijection. Thus the chosen beta depends on an established finite cardinality, not on an unsupported choice of lattice basis.

R003.fact: If b:I to M is an R-basis and beta:J to I is a bijection, then j maps to b(beta(j)) is an R-basis. Over a nonzero field every vector of a basis is nonzero.

grounds.reason: H007 provides bZ as an integer basis with the corresponding complex basis.
F001 provides the finite-cardinality bijection used for beta.
qBasis is the canonical K-basis supplied by base change, indexed by Fin(n), and n=ell+1 is positive.

R003.justification: Under a bijection, finite coordinate families are reindexed bijectively; spanning expansions and uniqueness of coefficients are preserved. If a basis vector were zero, the finite coefficient family with coefficient 1 at its index and 0 elsewhere would represent zero, contradicting uniqueness against the all-zero family. K is a field, so 1 differs from 0.

R003.fact: For an algebraic tensor product over Z, a biadditive Z-balanced rule into an abelian group extends uniquely to an additive map. Two additive maps agreeing on every pure tensor agree everywhere. For a fixed scalar, equality expressing K-linearity can likewise be checked on pure tensors when both sides are additive.

grounds.reason: The tensor products are algebraic, generated additively by pure tensors with additivity and Z-balancing relations.
U uses the corresponding first-factor K-action.
The formula for F(f) is biadditive and balanced because f is Z-linear.

R003.justification: Present the tensor product as the free abelian group on pairs modulo the biadditivity and balancing relations. Any rule satisfying those relations descends to the quotient. Every element is a finite integer combination of generators; integer coefficients can be absorbed into a tensor factor. Additivity therefore extends equality from pure tensors to all elements. Multiplication by a fixed K scalar is additive, so equality of the two additive maps in a scalar-compatibility identity can also be tested on generators. The later applications must, and do, check their particular formulas; the background fact itself uses only the supplied algebraic tensor-product definitions.

R003.fact: If S:A to B is a linear isomorphism, T:A to A and Q:B to B are linear, and ST=QS, then W maps to S(W) is a bijection between T-invariant subspaces of A and Q-invariant subspaces of B, with inverse Z maps to S_inv(Z). It sends zero and whole spaces to zero and whole spaces.

F(f) is a K-linear operator on U.
ind(f) is a K-linear operator on V_K.
For arbitrary f0, the displayed pure-tensor calculation proves S ind(f0)=F(f0) S everywhere.

R003.justification: The image of a subspace under a linear map is a subspace. If T(W) is contained in W, then Q(S(W))=S(T(W)) is contained in S(W). From ST=QS and the inverse identities one obtains T S_inv=S_inv Q, proving the converse for inverse images. The mutually inverse maps S and S_inv make these subspace assignments inverse bijections. Linearity sends zero to zero and surjectivity sends A onto B.

R004.fact: For the supplied unital ring homomorphism F:End_Z(M)→End_K(U), every integer t and f∈End_Z(M) satisfy F(t·f)=red(t)·F(f). For K-linear endomorphisms P,Q and scalars a,b∈K, (a·P)(b·Q)=(ab)·(PQ).

grounds.reason: F is explicitly a unital ring homomorphism with codomain End_K(U).
red is the canonical integer map into K.

R004.justification: For nonnegative t, additivity gives F(t·f)=t·F(f) by finite induction; preservation of negation extends this to integers. In End_K(U), this repeated integer addition equals multiplication by red(t), as seen on each vector. Also P(bQ(u))=bP(Q(u)) by K-linearity, so evaluation gives (aP)(bQ)(u)=ab(PQ)(u). These facts justify the scalar transfers and rearrangements used in S002 and again in S003.

R004.fact: For a K-linear subspace W of U, if P preserves W then P^s preserves W for every natural s. If P and Q preserve W, then PQ preserves W, and aP preserves W for every a∈K.

grounds.reason: W is an arbitrary K-linear subspace of U.
L2 assumes stability under F(x_M) and F(y_M); F003 supplies scalar-power formulas before they are used.
Stability means that each vector of W is mapped into W.
The divided-power formulas hold for all indices at most ell.

R004.justification: The identity preserves W. Inductively, P^(s+1)(w)=P(P^s(w)) lies in W. Similarly, PQ(w) lies in W by applying Q and then P, and aP(w) lies in W by closure of a K-subspace under scalar multiplication. Applying these facts to F003 and to the four factors displayed in S004 verifies precisely the stated stability step.

R005.fact: For a vector u≠0 in a vector space over a field k, a·u=0 implies a=0. For a finite index type I, a family b:I→U is linearly independent precisely when every relation ∑_{i∈I} a_i·b_i=0 has all a_i=0.

Linear independence means that the kernel of the map taking a finitely supported coefficient family to its linear combination is zero. On finite I every coefficient family is finitely supported and this map is the displayed finite sum. Thus the coefficient extraction in S005 proves the required independence.

R005.fact: If every vector b_i of a family belongs to a k-linear subspace W≤U, then span_k(range b)⊆W. Consequently, if that span equals U, then W=U.
